data.why: The app's own crystal dropdown fetches .cif files live from crystallography.net (no caching shipped in the repo), which the sandboxed server cannot reach; pre-seeding app/cif_files/ with standard, structurally-correct CIFs under the exact filenames the dropdown expects (Diamond=9012290.cif, Aluminium=9008460.cif, W=9006486.cif, Pb=1531228.cif) lets the code's 'skip download if file exists' branch succeed offline, and an extra NaCl CIF is provided as an upload test file to exercise the 'Upload a .cif file' path.

goals: Pick a crystal (built-in dropdown or upload a .cif) and an X-ray energy, and see whether enough flux is transmitted through a sample of given thickness to be usable for DF-XRM
Browse the table of allowed reflections (2-theta, intensity, d-spacing) for the chosen crystal and wavelength and pick a suitable Q-vector/reflection
See a 3D rendering of how the crystal, sample, beam, lens and goniometer must be oriented to satisfy the chosen reflection, and read off the goniometer angles needed for alignment
Change the sample's real/reciprocal-lattice facet directions ('up' and exit-surface vectors) and see the rendering and goniometer angles update
Optionally lay out the downstream optics (lens box) geometry for a chosen sample-detector distance and energy
Export the session as a PDF report or as a pickled/Blender 3D scene for later reference

review.summary: This is a faithful, well-evidenced tree that follows the README's own sequence from absorption check through reflection, orientation and lens box to export, and all eight screens I opened show exactly what their nodes claim. It frames the tool as pre-beamtime planning only, missing the paper's emphasis on communicating geometry during the experiment and analysis, and it should fold in the replay's caveats (silent nan angles, Q resets, lost sort) and add a crystal-loader feature before filing.
